title: Panel data and the 2×2 difference-in-differences
text:
The fixed-effects model
\[Y_{it} = \delta D_{it} + \mathbf{X}_{it}\beta + u_i + \varepsilon_{it}\]

\(u_i\): everything about unit \(i\) that does not change
It can be correlated with \(D_{it}\) however it likes
FE compares each unit to itself

title: Panel data and the 2×2 difference-in-differences
text:
Within vs between


Four units, each observed eight times. Across units the relationship looks positive; within every unit it is negative. Fixed effects keep only the within slopes — by unit dummies, by demeaning, or by differencing, all equivalent.

title: Panel data and the 2×2 difference-in-differences
text:
What FE needs

Strict exogeneity: \(E[\varepsilon_{it} \mid D_{i1}, \dots, D_{iT}, u_i] = 0\)
Time-varying unobservables that move with \(D\): still a problem
Feedback (today’s shock → tomorrow’s treatment): a problem
Regressors that never change within unit: absorbed, gone

title: Panel data and the 2×2 difference-in-differences
text:
The SASP question

Sex workers charge more for unprotected sex. Compensating differential, or selection?
Panel: same provider, many clients
Pooled OLS: premium ≈ 0. Within provider: ≈ 5%.

title: Panel data and the 2×2 difference-in-differences
text:
The 2×2 DiD
\[\hat{\delta} = (\bar{Y}_{T,post} - \bar{Y}_{T,pre}) - (\bar{Y}_{C,post} - \bar{Y}_{C,pre})\]

As a regression: \(Y = \alpha + \beta\,\text{Treat} + \gamma\,\text{Post} + \delta\,(\text{Treat} \times \text{Post}) + e\)
Assumption: parallel trends — a counterfactual claim, untestable in the 2×2

The dashed line is the assumption: without the move upstream, Lambeth would have risen by the same +12 as Southwark & Vauxhall. The effect is the gap between that line and what happened.

title: Regression discontinuity
text:
The design

Running variable \(X\), cutoff \(c_0\)
Sharp: \(D = 1[X \geq c_0]\)
Fuzzy: \(P(D = 1 \mid X)\) jumps at \(c_0\)
Units just above and just below differ in \(D\) and, if nothing else jumps, in nothing else

title: Regression discontinuity
section: The picture that is the argument

title: Regression discontinuity
text:
Identification by continuity
\[\delta_{SRD} = \lim_{x \downarrow c_0} E[Y \mid X = x] - \lim_{x \uparrow c_0} E[Y \mid X = x]\]

Assumption: \(E[Y^0 \mid X]\) and \(E[Y^1 \mid X]\) are continuous at \(c_0\)
No CIA, no need to observe confounders
Estimand is local to the cutoff

title: Regression discontinuity
text:
Estimation is bias vs variance


Each point is the same regression with a different window around the cutoff. rdrobust picks the window that balances the two errors.

title: Regression discontinuity
text:
Threats

Manipulation: units sort just past the cutoff → density jumps (McCrary / rddensity)
Something else at the cutoff: covariates should be smooth there
Wrong functional form: placebo cutoffs should show nothing

title: Potential outcomes
text:
Estimands

\(ATE = E[\delta]\)
\(ATT = E[\delta \mid D = 1]\)
\(ATU = E[\delta \mid D = 0]\)
They differ when effects are heterogeneous and treatment is selected on them

title: Potential outcomes
text:
The decomposition
\[\underbrace{E[Y \mid D=1] - E[Y \mid D=0]}_{\text{SDO}} = ATE + \underbrace{E[Y^0 \mid D=1] - E[Y^0 \mid D=0]}_{\text{selection bias}} + \underbrace{(1-\pi)(ATT - ATU)}_{\text{HTE bias}}\]

Selection bias: the treated would have done differently anyway
HTE bias: the treated gain differently from treatment
Every design in this book is a story about killing these two terms

Randomization inference

Fisher’s sharp null: \(\delta_i = 0\) for every \(i\)
Under it, every missing potential outcome is known
Recompute the statistic for every possible assignment
Exact \(p\)-value, no distributional assumptions, no large-sample appeal

Correlation is not causation — but why not?

People, firms and governments optimize
Observed outcomes are the result of choices made with information we do not see
So the treatment is correlated with everything that drove the choice
“Optimization makes everything endogenous”

Price elasticity of demand

Every observed (price, quantity) is an equilibrium: supply and demand moved
Regress \(Q\) on \(P\) and you get… a mix of both curves
Philip Wright (1928): find something that shifts supply only (weather)
That is the agenda for the whole book: where does the exogenous variation come from?

title: Why causal inference, and regression as a tool
text:
What a regression coefficient is

\(E[Y \mid X]\) is the conditional expectation function (CEF)
Regression gives the best linear approximation to the CEF, always
That is a descriptive fact. Nothing causal yet.
Causal content enters only through assumptions about \(u\): \(E[u \mid X] = 0\)

“Controlling for \(x_2\)” = using only the part of \(x_1\) that \(x_2\) cannot predict

title: Session 8 · Difference-in-differences, deep dive
text:
Key ideas
Event studies. With many periods, replace the single \(\text{Treat} \times \text{Post}\) with a full set of \(\text{Treat} \times \text{Year}\) interactions (omitting one reference year). The leads (pre-treatment interactions) should be near zero if parallel trends is plausible; the lags trace the dynamic effect. Passing a pre-trends test is not proof of parallel trends — the counterfactual is still unobserved — but failing it is close to disqualifying.






In plain English



Instead of one “after” effect, estimate a separate effect for every year: three years before the policy, two years before, the year of, the year after, and so on. The years before the policy are a sanity check — if the treated group was already pulling away before anything happened, the design is in trouble. The years after show the effect building or fading.


Placebos and triple differences (DDD). If theory says an effect should show up only for a specific group, cohort, or window, estimate the same model where it should not and demand a null. A DDD nets the placebo group’s DiD out of the treated group’s DiD, absorbing group-specific shocks that a plain DiD would attribute to treatment.






In plain English



A placebo test runs your analysis somewhere the policy couldn’t possibly have mattered — an older age group, a different outcome — and checks that you find nothing. A triple difference goes one step further and subtracts that placebo result from the real one, so anything weird that happened in those states in those years, affecting everyone, gets cancelled out.


The abortion study. Roe v. Wade legalized abortion nationally in 1973; five states had repealed their bans in 1970. Cohorts born 1971–1973 in repeal states were “treated” three years earlier than the rest of the country. If legalization reduced the share of unwanted births, those cohorts should show lower gonorrhea incidence as 15–19 year olds in 1986–1992, with the effect tracing a parabola as the treated cohort moves into and out of the age bracket. The placebo is 25–29 year olds in the same states.
Staggered adoption and two-way fixed effects (TWFE). With treatment switching on at different times for different units, the TWFE coefficient (unit fixed effects plus year fixed effects) is a variance-weighted average of every 2×2 DiD in the data (Goodman-Bacon 2021): early vs never-treated, late vs never-treated, early vs late (before late is treated), and late vs early (after early is treated). In that last type the “control” is already treated; if effects grow over time, its trend is contaminated and the 2×2 is biased — sometimes to the wrong sign. The decomposition tells you how much weight these comparisons get.






In plain English



When states adopt a law in different years, the standard regression quietly runs every possible two-group comparison and averages them. Some of those comparisons use a state that already has the law as the “control” for a state that is just getting it. If the law’s effect grows over time, the early state’s growing effect looks like a trend, gets subtracted, and the estimate shrinks or even flips sign. The Bacon decomposition shows you how much of your estimate rests on those bad comparisons.


Modern estimators. Callaway and Sant’Anna estimate each cohort-by-time average treatment effect on the treated (ATT) using only never-treated or not-yet-treated controls and aggregate them with transparent weights. Sun and Abraham do the analogous thing within an interaction-weighted event-study regression. Both avoid the forbidden comparisons; both need a clean control group.






In plain English



The newer methods just refuse to use already-treated units as a comparison group. They compare each adopting cohort to units that haven’t adopted yet (or never will), one period at a time, and then average those clean comparisons however you like. If you have plenty of never-treated units, they agree with the standard regression; if you don’t, they can differ a lot.

Step 1 — Abortion legalization: the DD event study
Black women aged 15–19; log gonorrhea rate; repeal marks the five early-repeal states. The reference year is 1985; controls and population weights follow the paper.

PythonR



import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

ab = pd.read_stata("data/abortion.dta", convert_categoricals=False)
yrs = list(range(1986, 2001))
ctrl = "acc + ir + pi + alcohol + crack + poverty + income + ur"
needed = ["lnr", "totpop", "fip", "year", "repeal",
          "acc", "ir", "pi", "alcohol", "crack", "poverty", "income", "ur"]

def event_study(df):
    df = df.dropna(subset=needed).copy()
    for y in yrs:
        df[f"rep_{y}"] = ((df.year == y) & (df.repeal == 1)).astype(int)
    f = "lnr ~ " + " + ".join(f"rep_{y}" for y in yrs) + " + C(fip) + C(year) + " + ctrl
    m = smf.wls(f, data=df, weights=df.totpop).fit(cov_type="cluster", cov_kwds={"groups": df["fip"]})
    out = pd.DataFrame({"coef": m.params[[f"rep_{y}" for y in yrs]].to_numpy(),
                        "se":   m.bse[[f"rep_{y}" for y in yrs]].to_numpy()}, index=yrs)
    return out

bf15 = ab[(ab.sex == 2) & (ab.race == 2) & (ab.age == 15)]     # black females 15–19
dd = event_study(bf15)

Step 4 — Decompose the TWFE estimate into its 2×2s
The exact Goodman-Bacon decomposition needs a balanced panel, a binary treatment and no weights, so this step uses the unweighted binary version. In R, bacondecomp does it in one line; in Python we compute the 2×2 estimates and their weights by hand from the paper’s formulas.

Dbar = {g: (np.array(years) >= g).mean() if g > 0 else 0 for g in n.index}  # share of periods treated

def dd_2x2(sub):
    """TWFE on a two-group subsample = the 2x2 DD for that comparison."""
    s = sub.copy()
    for v in ["D", "l_homicide"]:
        s[v + "_t"] = s[v] - s.groupby("sid")[v].transform("mean") - s.groupby("year")[v].transform("mean") + s[v].mean()
    return (s.D_t * s.l_homicide_t).sum() / (s.D_t ** 2).sum()

rows = []
G = [g for g in n.index if g > 0]
for k in G:
    rows.append((k, "never-treated", dd_2x2(castle[castle.g.isin([k, 0])]),
                 n[k] * n[0] * Dbar[k] * (1 - Dbar[k])))
    for l in G:
        if l <= k: continue
        nkl = n[k] / (n[k] + n[l])
        # k treated earlier; l (not yet treated) is the control in years before l adopts
        s_kl = ((n[k] + n[l]) * (1 - Dbar[l]))**2 * nkl * (1 - nkl) * (Dbar[k] - Dbar[l]) / (1 - Dbar[l]) * (1 - Dbar[k]) / (1 - Dbar[l])
        rows.append((k, f"later-treated ({l}) as control", dd_2x2(castle[castle.g.isin([k, l]) & (castle.year < l)]), s_kl))
        # l treated later; k (already treated) is the control in years from k's adoption on
        s_lk = ((n[k] + n[l]) * Dbar[k])**2 * nkl * (1 - nkl) * Dbar[l] / Dbar[k] * (Dbar[k] - Dbar[l]) / Dbar[k]
        rows.append((l, f"earlier-treated ({k}) as control", dd_2x2(castle[castle.g.isin([k, l]) & (castle.year >= k)]), s_lk))

Solutions






Solutions (click to expand)





1. Each coefficient is now the repeal-vs-Roe gap in year \(t\) relative to the gap in 1990. Since 1990 is mid-treatment, the “pre-period” coefficients for 1986–1989 are differences between two treated years and no longer test for differential pre-trends; the only clean reference is a year before anyone was treated.
2. With no never-treated units and growing effects, the late-vs-early comparisons receive substantial weight and have negative 2×2 estimates (the early cohort’s growing effect is differenced out as a “trend”); TWFE badly understates the true average effect (in the simulation below the true average effect among treated observations is 1.5, TWFE gives ≈ 0.35 with no never-treated units) and can flip sign when the dynamic is steep. Adding 20 never-treated units pulls TWFE to ≈ 0.9 — better, still biased, because the forbidden comparisons still get weight; a Callaway–Sant’Anna aggregate would recover 1.5.
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
def panel(n_never):
    units = [(i, 4) for i in range(20)] + [(i, 7) for i in range(20, 40)] + [(i, 0) for i in range(40, 40 + n_never)]
    rows = [(i, g, t, (g > 0 and t >= g) * (t - g + 1) * 0.5 + rng.normal()) for i, g in units for t in range(10)]
    df = pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["sid", "g", "year", "l_homicide"])
    df["D"] = ((df.g > 0) & (df.year >= df.g)).astype(int)
    return df
for n_never in [0, 20]:
    df = panel(n_never)
    print(n_never, smf.ols("l_homicide ~ D + C(sid) + C(year)", df).fit().params["D"].round(3))
# then re-run the Step 4 decomposition on `df`

Facilitator notes






Facilitator notes (click to expand)





The event-study figure is the deliverable. Make sure every participant can produce Step 1’s plot and read it: leads, reference year, dynamics, confidence band. Everything in modern DiD is a conversation about that picture.
Misconception: flat pre-trends prove parallel trends. They make it more plausible. The counterfactual post-period trend is unobserved, full stop. Use the DDD to show what further evidence looks like.
Misconception: TWFE is “wrong.” It is a weighted average with weights you did not choose. With a big never-treated group it is fine (Step 4). Without one, it can be badly wrong (Exercise 2). The decomposition is how you tell.
On the Python decomposition. It follows Goodman-Bacon (2021) Theorem 1 and reproduces the TWFE coefficient to four decimals; that equality is the check that the code is right. It assumes a balanced panel, binary treatment and no weights, which is why Step 4 switches to the unweighted D.

title: Session 6 · Instrumental variables
text:
Key ideas
The problem IV solves. \(Y = \alpha + \delta D + u\) with \(\mathrm{Cov}(D, u) \neq 0\). Regression cannot recover \(\delta\). But if some instrumental variable (IV) \(Z\) moves \(D\) and is otherwise unrelated to \(Y\), then the only reason \(Y\) moves with \(Z\) is through \(D\), so \[\delta_{IV} = \frac{\mathrm{Cov}(Z, Y)}{\mathrm{Cov}(Z, D)} = \frac{\text{reduced form}}{\text{first stage}}.\]






In plain English



You can’t trust the raw relationship between schooling and wages because ambitious people get more of both. But suppose some people happened to grow up near a college. That nudges them toward more schooling, and — if it has no other effect on wages — any wage difference between near-college and far-from-college people must have come through schooling. Divide the wage gap by the schooling gap and you have the effect of schooling.


The conditions. Relevance: \(Z\) predicts \(D\) (testable; look at the first-stage F). Exclusion: \(Z\) affects \(Y\) only through \(D\) (untestable; argued from the DAG). Independence: \(Z\) is as good as random with respect to \(u\) (untestable). Philip Wright’s 1928 appendix is the origin story: identify a demand curve with a supply shifter (weather) that does not enter demand.






In plain English



An instrument has one job and one restriction. The job: it has to actually move the treatment (you can check this). The restriction: it must not touch the outcome any other way, and it must not itself be chosen by people for reasons related to the outcome (you cannot check either; you have to argue them). Most IV debates are about the restriction.


Two-stage least squares (2SLS). Regress \(D\) on \(Z\) and covariates, take the fitted values \(\hat{D}\), regress \(Y\) on \(\hat{D}\) and the same covariates. The second-stage standard errors must account for the first stage; use a proper IV routine, not two lm calls.
Weak instruments. When the first stage is weak, 2SLS is biased toward OLS and its sampling distribution is badly behaved. The rule of thumb is first-stage F above 10 for one endogenous regressor; the modern advice is to report it, prefer just-identified models, and be nervous below 20.






In plain English



If the instrument barely nudges the treatment, you are dividing a small number by another small number, and the answer swings wildly — and, worse, tends to drift back toward the naive estimate you were trying to avoid. The first-stage F-statistic measures how hard the nudge is; under 10 is a warning light.


Local average treatment effect (LATE). With heterogeneous effects, IV identifies the average effect for compliers — units whose treatment is moved by the instrument — under monotonicity (no defiers). Different instruments identify different LATEs for the same treatment. The judge-leniency design makes this vivid: the compliers are defendants who would be detained by a strict judge and released by a lenient one.






In plain English



IV only tells you about the people the instrument actually moved. Growing up near a college changes the plans of some teenagers and not others; the IV estimate is the return to schooling for those teenagers, not for everyone. A different instrument moves different people and can honestly give a different answer. “Local” means “for the movers.”

1. With both instruments the estimate rises to ≈ 0.16 (SE ≈ 0.05) and the first-stage F is ≈ 19; the Sargan statistic is 3.6 on 1 df, \(p ≈ 0.06\) — borderline. A rejection would say the two instruments imply different LATEs, which could be heterogeneity rather than invalidity; the test can never validate the exclusion restriction of either instrument on its own.
2. OLS is ≈ 1.8 regardless of \(\pi\) (the endogeneity bias). At \(\pi = 0.05\) the median first-stage F is ≈ 1 and the 2SLS median is ≈ 1.3 with an interquartile range of about 0.8–1.7, pulled toward OLS; at \(\pi = 0.1\) (F ≈ 5) the median is right but the IQR is still 0.6–1.3; by \(\pi = 0.2\) (F ≈ 20) it is tight around 1 (IQR 0.8–1.1). The F ≈ 10 threshold is where the worst behavior fades, not where it ends.
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
def sim(pi, n=500):
    z = rng.normal(size=n); uv = rng.multivariate_normal([0,0], [[1,.8],[.8,1]], n)

    fs = smf.ols("d ~ z", df).fit()
    return smf.ols("y ~ d", df).fit().params["d"], \

3. With D = educ >= 13, the first stage on nearc4 is about 0.06, i.e. roughly 6% of the sample are compliers. Using the ratio-of-first-stages method (\(P(x=1 \mid \text{complier}) / P(x=1) = \text{FS}_{x=1} / \text{FS}\)), compliers are far less likely to be Black (ratio ≈ 0.2) and less likely to be Southern (ratio ≈ 0.6) than the full sample. title: Session 4 · Matching and subclassification
text:
Key ideas
Conditional independence assumption (CIA). \((Y^0, Y^1) \perp D \mid X\). Within strata of \(X\), treatment is as good as random. This is the backdoor criterion in potential-outcomes clothing; it is also called selection on observables. It is an assumption about unobservables, so no test on the data can confirm it; only the DAG argument can.






In plain English



The bet behind matching: “once I line up people with the same age, education, and past earnings, the ones who got the program and the ones who didn’t are interchangeable.” If something you can’t see — motivation, say — also drove who signed up, the bet is lost, and no amount of data will tell you so.


Common support. \(0 < P(D=1 \mid X) < 1\). For each covariate profile there must be both treated and untreated units; otherwise you are extrapolating.






In plain English



You can only compare like with like if both kinds exist. If every 50-year-old in the data got the program, you have nobody to compare them to, and any “effect” for 50-year-olds is a guess. Check the overlap before you do anything else.


Subclassification. Stratify on \(X\), compute the treated-minus-control difference within each stratum, and average using the treated group’s stratum shares (for the average treatment effect on the treated, ATT). It works beautifully with a few discrete covariates and dies of the curse of dimensionality quickly.






In plain English



Sort people into bins — men/women, adult/child — compare treated to untreated inside each bin, then average the bin-by-bin gaps, counting each bin as heavily as it appears in the treated group. Simple and transparent, but with ten characteristics you have thousands of bins and most are empty.


Propensity score. Rosenbaum and Rubin: if CIA holds given \(X\), it also holds given \(p(X) = P(D=1 \mid X)\). One scalar replaces the whole covariate vector. Estimate it with a logit, then stratify on it, weight by it (inverse probability weighting, IPW), or match on it (nearest neighbor, NN).






In plain English



Instead of matching on ten characteristics at once, boil them down to one number: how likely was this person to get the treatment, given everything we know about them? Two people with the same likelihood are a fair comparison even if they got there by different routes. IPW uses that number as a weight; matching uses it to find each treated person’s closest untreated twin.


Dehejia–Wahba. LaLonde showed that regressions using a non-experimental control group (the Current Population Survey, CPS) badly missed the National Supported Work (NSW) experimental estimate. Dehejia and Wahba showed that propensity-score methods with a well-specified score and attention to common support get close. The lesson is double-edged: matching can work, and it can fail silently.






In plain English



A famous test case: a real experiment said job training raised earnings by about $1,800. Replacing the experiment’s control group with ordinary survey respondents gave minus $8,500. Careful propensity-score work got back to roughly $2,000. The method can rescue a bad comparison group — but only when you have the right variables, and nothing warns you when you don’t.

Then compute the bias-corrected matching estimate using a regression of \(Y\) on \(X\) in the control group. Compare all three to each other.
Trimming sensitivity. Rerun Step 4 with overlap windows (0.05, 0.95), (0.1, 0.9) and (0.2, 0.8). How does the estimate and the sample size move? Write two sentences on the bias–variance trade-off involved.

title: Session 4 · Matching and subclassification
text:
Solutions






Solutions (click to expand)





1. Raw SDO = 3.25. Matching each treated unit to the control with the closest X (11→10, 7→8, 5→4, 3→4) gives an ATT of 2.25. The bias-corrected version adjusts each matched pair by \(\hat{\mu}_0(X_{treated}) - \hat{\mu}_0(X_{match})\), where \(\hat{\mu}_0\) is the control-group regression of \(Y\) on \(X\). In this tiny example the \(X\) mismatches are +1, −1, +1, −1, so with a linear \(\hat{\mu}_0\) the corrections cancel and the bias-corrected ATT is also 2.25 — which is itself a useful lesson: the correction matters when mismatches are systematic, not when they are balanced.
tb = pd.read_stata("data/training_bias_reduction.dta")
tr, co = tb[tb.D == 1], tb[tb.D == 0]
mu0 = smf.ols("Y ~ X", co).fit()
rows = []
for _, r in tr.iterrows():
    j = (co.X - r.X).abs().idxmin()
    rows.append((r.Y - co.loc[j, "Y"],
                 r.Y - co.loc[j, "Y"] - (mu0.predict(pd.DataFrame({"X":[r.X]}))[0]
                                        - mu0.predict(pd.DataFrame({"X":[co.loc[j,"X"]]}))[0])))
print(np.mean(rows, axis=0))   # [naive NN ATT, bias-corrected ATT]
2. (0.05, 0.95): ≈ +$1,320 on 601 units; (0.1, 0.9): ≈ +$2,030 on 445; (0.2, 0.8): ≈ +$3,210 on 256. Wider windows keep more controls (lower variance) but include units with poor overlap (more bias); narrower windows do the reverse. The estimate swings by almost $2,000 across reasonable choices — report the sensitivity, not one number.
3. Without lagged earnings the treated group’s mean score drops from 0.33 to about 0.20, and the (0.1, 0.9) IPW estimate flips to ≈ −$2,080. The score no longer captures the dimension that matters most (NSW enrollees had near-zero 1974–75 earnings). Pre-treatment outcomes are the single most important covariate in this design.

title: Session 2 · Directed acyclic graphs
text:
Key ideas
A directed acyclic graph (DAG) is a set of causal claims, including the arrows you leave out. Nodes are variables; a directed edge \(A \to B\) says \(A\) causes \(B\); the absence of an edge is the strong claim that there is no direct effect. “Acyclic” means you can never follow arrows in a loop back to where you started. The DAG encodes your prior knowledge of the data-generating process — theory, institutional detail, previous studies — and that is what makes it useful: it forces you to write down what you believe before you touch data.






In plain English



A DAG is a sketch of your story about how the world works: boxes for the things you measure, arrows for “this one causes that one.” Drawing it before you run anything makes your assumptions visible, which is the point — you can argue about a picture, but you can’t argue about an assumption nobody wrote down.


Paths and what blocks them. A backdoor path from \(D\) to \(Y\) is any path starting with an arrow into \(D\). Backdoor paths carry non-causal association. A path is blocked if it contains a non-collider you condition on, or a collider you do not condition on. A collider is a node where two arrows meet (\(A \to C \leftarrow B\)). Conditioning on a collider (or its descendant) opens the path.






In plain English



Think of paths as pipes that can carry a fake correlation from the treatment to the outcome. A confounder (a common cause of both) is a pipe that is open by default; you close it by controlling for the confounder. A collider (something caused by both) is a pipe that is closed by default; controlling for it opens the pipe. Same action, opposite effect, depending only on which way the arrows point.


The backdoor criterion. A set of variables \(X\) satisfies the backdoor criterion for \((D, Y)\) if \(X\) blocks every backdoor path and contains no descendant of \(D\). Then conditioning on \(X\) identifies the causal effect of \(D\) on \(Y\). This is the formal version of “conditional independence” and “selection on observables” that Sessions 4 and 7 rely on.






In plain English



The backdoor criterion is a checklist for what to put in your regression: enough variables to close every fake pipe, and nothing that sits downstream of the treatment. It can say “control for nothing” (if the treatment was randomized) or “you cannot fix this with controls at all” (if a confounder is unmeasured). Both are legitimate answers.


Collider bias is the chapter’s main warning. The book’s discrimination example: female \(\to\) discrimination \(\to\) occupation \(\to\) wage, with discrimination \(\to\) wage directly and unobserved ability \(\to\) occupation and ability \(\to\) wage. Occupation is a collider on the path discrimination \(\to\) occupation \(\leftarrow\) ability \(\to\) wage. “Controlling for occupation,” which sounds like good practice, opens that path and makes discrimination look like it raises wages. The second example — a negative talent–beauty correlation among movie stars when both are independent in the population — is the same mechanism via sample selection.






In plain English



Suppose discrimination pushes women out of high-paying jobs, and high-ability people get into them. Among women in a given job, the ones who made it there against the headwind tend to be unusually able — and are paid for it. Comparing men and women within the same job therefore makes discrimination look harmless or even helpful. The job variable is the collider; comparing “within” it is the mistake.

text:
Exercises

Draw before you regress. A study finds that among hospitalized patients, smoking is negatively associated with COVID-19 severity. Draw a DAG in which smoking does not protect against severe illness but this association appears anyway. Simulate it and show the sign reversal.
Mediator or collider? In the Step 1 DGP, change occupation so that it is caused by female directly (set the 0 * female coefficient to −1) rather than only through discrimination. Re-run the three regressions. Which coefficients change, which do not, and why does the backdoor criterion still give the same answer for the total effect?
Bad controls in the wild. Find one published or newsroom regression (any field) that controls for something plausibly downstream of the treatment. Draw its DAG, and write three sentences on whether the control is a mediator, a collider, or harmless.

title: Session 2 · Directed acyclic graphs
text:
Solutions






Solutions (click to expand)





1. One DAG: smoking → hospitalization ← severity (both smoking-related illness and severe COVID get you admitted), with smoking having no arrow to severity. Restricting the sample to the hospitalized conditions on the collider.
rng = np.random.default_rng(7); n = 100_000
smoke = rng.binomial(1, 0.3, n)
severity = rng.normal(size=n)                      # independent of smoking
hosp = (0.8*smoke + severity + rng.normal(size=n)) > 1.0
d = pd.DataFrame(dict(smoke=smoke, severity=severity, hosp=hosp))
print(smf.ols("severity ~ smoke", d).fit().params["smoke"])            # ≈ 0
print(smf.ols("severity ~ smoke", d[d.hosp]).fit().params["smoke"])    # < 0
2. The unconditional female coefficient becomes more negative, ≈ −4 (−1 direct via discrimination, −2 via discrimination→occupation, and now −1 more via female→occupation); the collider regression is now ≈ +1.4, even more misleading; the full regression still returns ≈ −1. The collider regression is still wrong, and the full regression now returns the direct effect of female holding occupation fixed, which is −1 (through discrimination). The total effect is still identified with no controls because there are still no arrows into female: randomness of the treatment is what makes the empty adjustment set valid.
3. Open-ended. Common finds: wage regressions that control for occupation or industry; health studies that control for BMI when the treatment affects weight; education studies controlling for test scores measured after the intervention.

Facilitator notes (click to expand)





Make them draw. The biggest failure mode of this session is treating the DAG as decoration for a regression someone already planned. Have each participant sketch the discrimination DAG on paper before Step 2 and predict the sign of the collider regression. Most will predict it stays negative.

title: Glossary
section: Sessions 1–3: the vocabulary of causal questions
text:
Sessions 1–3: the vocabulary of causal questions
Treatment (\(D\)). The thing whose effect you want to know: a policy, a program, a drug, a price change. \(D = 1\) for units that got it, \(D = 0\) for units that did not.
Outcome (\(Y\)). The thing you measure to see whether the treatment did anything.
Potential outcomes (\(Y^1\), \(Y^0\)). For one unit, the outcome it would have under treatment (\(Y^1\)) and the outcome it would have without treatment (\(Y^0\)). You only ever see one of the two. The unseen one is the counterfactual.
Treatment effect (\(\delta_i\)). For one unit, \(Y_i^1 - Y_i^0\). Never directly observable, which is why everything below is about averages.
ATE — Average Treatment Effect. The average of \(\delta_i\) over everyone in the population. “If we treated everybody versus nobody, how much would the outcome change on average?”
ATT — Average Treatment effect on the Treated. The average of \(\delta_i\) over the units that actually got the treatment. “For the people who took the program, how much did it help them?”
ATU — Average Treatment effect on the Untreated. The average of \(\delta_i\) over the units that did not get the treatment. “If we had given the program to the people who didn’t get it, how much would it have helped them?” ATE is a weighted mix of ATT and ATU.
SDO — Simple Difference in Outcomes. The average outcome of the treated group minus the average outcome of the untreated group. It is what a naive comparison gives you. It equals the ATE only if the two groups were comparable to begin with.
Selection bias. The part of the SDO that comes from the treated and untreated groups being different people, not from the treatment. Formally: \(E[Y^0 \mid D=1] - E[Y^0 \mid D=0]\), the gap in how the two groups would have done without treatment.
HTE — Heterogeneous Treatment Effects. The treatment helps some units more than others. “HTE bias” is the extra error in the SDO that appears when the people who got treated are the ones it helps most (or least).
Endogenous / exogenous. A variable is endogenous if it is determined inside the system you are studying — chosen by someone, or caused by something that also affects the outcome. It is exogenous if it came from outside, like a coin flip. Causal inference is the hunt for exogenous variation in the treatment.
RCT — Randomized Controlled Trial. An experiment where a coin flip (or equivalent) decides who gets treated. Randomization makes the treatment exogenous.
RI — Randomization Inference. A way of testing whether an effect could be luck: pretend the treatment did nothing, reshuffle who was “treated” many times, and see how often the reshuffled data produce an effect as big as the real one.
Sharp null. The specific hypothesis RI tests: the treatment effect is exactly zero for every single unit, not just on average.
CEF — Conditional Expectation Function. \(E[Y \mid X]\): the average of \(Y\) among units with a given value of \(X\). Regression is a way of approximating this function with a line (or a plane).
OLS — Ordinary Least Squares. The standard way of fitting a regression line: choose the line that makes the squared gaps between the data and the line as small as possible.
SE — Standard Error. How much an estimate would bounce around if you could redo the study with a fresh sample. Small SE means a precise estimate. “Robust” SEs allow the noise to differ across units; “clustered” SEs allow units in the same group (same school, same state) to share noise.
Regression anatomy / FWL — Frisch–Waugh–Lovell. The rule that a coefficient in a multiple regression equals the simple regression of \(Y\) on the leftover part of that variable after removing what the other variables predict. It is what “controlling for” means mechanically.
DAG — Directed Acyclic Graph. A diagram of arrows showing which variables cause which. “Directed” because arrows have a direction; “acyclic” because you can never follow arrows in a loop back to where you started.
Confounder. A variable that causes both the treatment and the outcome. It creates a fake association unless you adjust for it.
Collider. A variable that is caused by both of two other variables (two arrows collide into it). Adjusting for a collider creates a fake association that was not there before.
Backdoor path / backdoor criterion. A backdoor path is any route from treatment to outcome that starts with an arrow pointing into the treatment; it carries non-causal association. The backdoor criterion says which variables to adjust for so that every such path is blocked.

title: Glossary
text:
Sessions 4–6: designs for cross-sectional data
CIA — Conditional Independence Assumption. Once you account for the observed variables \(X\), who got treated is as good as random. Also called selection on observables or unconfoundedness. It is an assumption about things you cannot see, so it cannot be tested.
Common support / overlap. For every type of unit (every value of \(X\)), there are both treated and untreated examples. Without it you are guessing about people who have no comparison.
Subclassification / stratification. Split the data into groups with the same \(X\), compare treated and untreated within each group, then average the comparisons.
Propensity score. The probability that a unit gets treated, given its characteristics \(X\). Usually estimated with a logistic regression. Two units with the same score are comparable even if their individual characteristics differ.
IPW — Inverse Probability Weighting. Reweight the data so that the treated and untreated groups look alike: treated units get weight \(1/p\), untreated units get weight \(1/(1-p)\), where \(p\) is the propensity score.
Matching / NN — Nearest Neighbor. For each treated unit, find the untreated unit that looks most like it (by \(X\) or by propensity score) and compare the two.
RD / RDD — Regression Discontinuity (Design). A design that uses a cutoff rule: units just above and just below a threshold get different treatments but are otherwise alike.
Running variable. The variable with the cutoff in it (a test score, a vote share, an age). Also called the forcing or assignment variable.
Sharp vs fuzzy RD. Sharp: crossing the cutoff always changes treatment. Fuzzy: crossing the cutoff changes the probability of treatment.
Bandwidth (\(h\)). How far on either side of the cutoff you look. Narrower is more credible but noisier.
Local linear regression. Fit a straight line separately on each side of the cutoff, using only data within the bandwidth, and measure the jump between the two lines at the cutoff.
McCrary density test. A check for cheating at the cutoff: if units can push themselves just past the threshold, there will be a pile-up on one side.
IV — Instrumental Variable. A variable that moves the treatment but has no other way of affecting the outcome. It lets you isolate the part of the treatment that is as good as random.
Relevance, exclusion, independence. The three conditions an instrument must satisfy: it actually moves the treatment (relevance, testable); it affects the outcome only through the treatment (exclusion, not testable); it is itself as good as random (independence, not testable).
First stage. The regression of treatment on the instrument. Its coefficient tells you how strongly the instrument moves treatment.
Reduced form. The regression of the outcome on the instrument. Dividing reduced form by first stage gives the IV estimate (the Wald ratio).
2SLS — Two-Stage Least Squares. The standard IV estimator: stage one predicts the treatment from the instrument; stage two regresses the outcome on that prediction.
Weak instrument. An instrument that barely moves the treatment. The symptom is a small first-stage F-statistic (under about 10); the consequence is an estimate biased toward the naive one and unreliable confidence intervals.
LATE — Local Average Treatment Effect. What IV actually estimates when effects differ across people: the average effect for compliers, the units whose treatment was changed by the instrument.
Compliers, always-takers, never-takers, defiers. Compliers take the treatment when the instrument says to and not otherwise. Always-takers and never-takers ignore the instrument. Defiers do the opposite of what the instrument says; monotonicity is the assumption that there are none.

title: Glossary
section: Sessions 7–9: designs for data over time
text:
Sessions 7–9: designs for data over time
Panel data. The same units observed repeatedly over time (the same people every year, the same states every quarter).
FE — Fixed Effects. A regression that gives every unit its own intercept, so that anything about the unit that never changes is automatically accounted for. Equivalent to comparing each unit only with itself over time.
Within vs between variation. Within: how a unit changes over time. Between: how units differ from each other. FE uses only the within part.
Strict exogeneity. The assumption FE needs: the unexplained noise in any period is unrelated to the treatment in every period, past and future.
DiD / DD — Difference-in-Differences. Compare the change over time in a treated group with the change over time in an untreated group. The second difference removes trends that both groups share.
Parallel trends. The assumption DiD needs: without the treatment, the treated group would have moved over time the same way the control group did.
2×2. The simplest DiD: two groups (treated, control) and two periods (before, after).
Event study. A DiD with a separate effect estimated for each period relative to when treatment started, so you can see effects building up or fading, and check that nothing was happening before treatment.
Leads and lags. In an event study, leads are the pre-treatment periods (they should show no effect); lags are the post-treatment periods (they show the dynamic effect).
Placebo test. Run the same analysis on a group, period, or outcome where the treatment should have had no effect, and check that you find nothing.
DDD — Triple Difference. A DiD of two DiDs: the treated group’s DiD minus a placebo group’s DiD. It removes shocks specific to the treated group’s location or time that a plain DiD would mistake for the treatment.
TWFE — Two-Way Fixed Effects. A regression with both unit fixed effects and time fixed effects. The standard way to run DiD with many units and periods.
Staggered adoption. Different units start treatment at different times.
Bacon decomposition (Goodman-Bacon). A way of breaking a staggered TWFE estimate into all the simple 2×2 comparisons it secretly averages, with their weights. It reveals when TWFE is comparing late-treated units to already-treated ones, which can bias the result.
Callaway–Sant’Anna, Sun–Abraham. Newer DiD estimators that avoid using already-treated units as controls.
Synthetic control. For one treated unit (a state, a country), build a “synthetic” version from a weighted average of untreated units, choosing weights so the synthetic version matches the real one before treatment. The post-treatment gap is the effect.
Donor pool. The untreated units available to build the synthetic control from.
RMSPE — Root Mean Squared Prediction Error. How far the synthetic unit is from the real one, on average. Pre-period RMSPE measures fit quality; the post/pre ratio is used for inference.
Placebo-in-space / placebo-in-time. Re-run the synthetic control pretending a different unit was treated (in space) or that treatment happened at an earlier date (in time). If the real result is not unusual compared to the placebos, it is probably noise.

title: Session 1 · Why causal inference, and regression as a tool
text:
Key ideas
Optimization makes everything endogenous. The book’s opening example is price elasticity of demand. Observed prices and quantities are equilibrium outcomes: both supply and demand shifted to produce every point you see, so a regression of quantity on price identifies nothing unless something moved only one curve. Wright’s instrumental-variables solution (Session 6) is the first sighting of the whole book’s agenda: find variation in the cause that is unrelated to everything else that matters. A variable is endogenous when it is chosen or caused by something inside the system you are studying, and exogenous when it comes from outside, like a coin flip.






In plain English



People, companies and governments make choices for reasons. If you compare the people who chose something with the people who didn’t, you are also comparing their reasons — and the reasons usually affect the outcome too. So “people who did X did better” rarely tells you that X helped. The whole book is a search for situations where who got X was decided by something close to a coin flip.


Regression estimates a conditional expectation function (CEF), not a causal effect. The CEF, \(E[Y \mid X]\), is the average of \(Y\) among units with a given \(X\). Chapter 2 builds up to three theorems. The linear CEF theorem says if the CEF is linear, regression recovers it. The best linear predictor theorem says regression is always the best linear approximation to the CEF, whether or not it is linear. The regression CEF theorem says regression also gives the best linear approximation to the CEF itself. None of these say anything about causation; they say what the numbers mean descriptively. Causal content enters only through assumptions about the error term (mean independence, \(E[u \mid x] = 0\)), and those assumptions are what the rest of the book is about.






In plain English



A regression line is a summary of averages: “among cars of this length, the average price is about this much.” That is a true and useful description. It becomes a statement about cause only if you add an assumption — that nothing else which matters for price is tangled up with length. Regression software never checks that assumption; you have to argue it.


Regression anatomy. The coefficient on \(x_1\) in a multiple regression equals the bivariate regression of \(y\) on the residual from regressing \(x_1\) on the other covariates: \[\beta_1 = \frac{\mathrm{Cov}(y, \tilde{x}_1)}{\mathrm{Var}(\tilde{x}_1)}, \qquad \tilde{x}_1 = x_1 - \hat{E}[x_1 \mid x_2, \dots, x_k].\] This is the Frisch–Waugh–Lovell (FWL) theorem, and it is the single most useful mechanical fact about regression: “controlling for” means “using only the part of \(x_1\) that the controls cannot predict.”






In plain English



“Controlling for weight” sounds like magic, but it is a two-step recipe: first figure out how much of a car’s length you could have guessed from its weight, throw that part away, and keep only the leftover “surprise” in length. Then see how price moves with that leftover. The coefficient in the big regression is exactly that.


Standard errors. A standard error (SE) says how much an estimate would bounce around in a fresh sample. Conventional ordinary least squares (OLS) standard errors assume homoskedasticity — the same amount of noise for every unit. Heteroskedasticity-robust (HC1, Stata’s robust) standard errors do not. When observations share a shock (students in the same classroom, firms in the same state), errors are correlated within groups and you need cluster-robust standard errors; the robust-versus-conventional gap on a single regression is a diagnostic, not a decision rule.






In plain English



The estimate is your best guess; the standard error is how shaky that guess is. The default formula assumes every observation is equally noisy and independent of the others. “Robust” relaxes the first part; “clustered” relaxes the second, for cases where units come in groups that share luck — kids in one classroom, counties in one state. Neither one changes the guess itself, only how confident you should be.

title: Session 1 · Why causal inference, and regression as a tool
text:
Solutions






Solutions (click to expand)





1. For mpg: residualize mpg on length + weight + headroom, regress price on the residual; slope is −87.96. For weight: residualize on length + headroom + mpg; slope is 4.34. Compare each residual’s variance to the variable’s raw variance: mpg keeps about 34% of its variation after partialling out the others, while length and weight each keep only about 10% (they are nearly collinear with one another). Precision is \(\sigma^2 / (n \cdot \mathrm{Var}(\tilde{x}_k))\) scaled by the variable’s units, so the coefficient whose regressor retains the most of its own variation — mpg — is the one estimated most precisely relative to its scale; length and weight are fighting over the same variation.
2. Stay wins ≈ 1/3, switch wins ≈ 2/3. With a random host (void if the car is revealed), both strategies win 1/2 of the non-void games. The informed host’s choice is a function of where the car is, so conditioning on it moves probability; the random host’s choice is independent of the car’s location, so it carries no information.
rng = np.random.default_rng(0); N = 100_000
car = rng.integers(0, 3, N); pick = rng.integers(0, 3, N)
# informed host opens a goat door that is not the pick
host = np.array([next(d for d in rng.permutation(3) if d != c and d != p) for c, p in zip(car, pick)])
switch = 3 - pick - host
print((pick == car).mean(), (switch == car).mean())
3. Homoskedastic case: the two SEs agree to two decimals. At n = 50 the robust SE has a noticeably larger spread across replications (it estimates more parameters from the same data). Researchers accept the variability because the robust estimator is consistent under a wider set of DGPs, but with tiny samples HC2/HC3 corrections are advisable.

title: Session 3 · Potential outcomes
text:
Key ideas
Potential outcomes. Each unit \(i\) has \(Y_i^1\) (outcome if treated) and \(Y_i^0\) (if not). The individual treatment effect is \(\delta_i = Y_i^1 - Y_i^0\). We observe only \(Y_i = D_i Y_i^1 + (1 - D_i) Y_i^0\) — the switching equation. The missing potential outcome is the fundamental problem of causal inference; every design in this book is a strategy for filling it in credibly.






In plain English



For any one person there are two possible futures — with the treatment and without — and you only get to watch one. The effect on that person is the gap between the two futures, which you can never see directly. Every method in this book is a trick for estimating the future you didn’t get to watch, using other people who did.


Estimands. The average treatment effect, \(ATE = E[\delta]\), averages over everyone. The average treatment effect on the treated, \(ATT = E[\delta \mid D = 1]\), averages over the units that actually got treated. The average treatment effect on the untreated, \(ATU = E[\delta \mid D = 0]\), averages over those that did not. They differ whenever effects are heterogeneous and treatment is selected on them.






In plain English



ATE: “How much would it help on average if we gave it to everyone?” ATT: “How much did it help the people who actually got it?” ATU: “How much would it have helped the people who didn’t?” These can be very different numbers — a job-training program might help the people who sign up (ATT) a lot more than it would help a random person (ATE).


The decomposition. The simple difference in outcomes (SDO) — the treated group’s average minus the untreated group’s — is \[E[Y \mid D=1] - E[Y \mid D=0] = ATE + \underbrace{E[Y^0 \mid D=1] - E[Y^0 \mid D=0]}_{\text{selection bias}} + \underbrace{(1-\pi)(ATT - ATU)}_{\text{heterogeneous-effect (HTE) bias}}.\] Selection bias: treated units would have done differently even untreated. HTE bias: treated units gain differently from treatment. Randomization makes \(D\) independent of \((Y^0, Y^1)\), so both bias terms are zero and the SDO is the ATE.






In plain English



Comparing treated and untreated averages gives you the true effect plus two kinds of junk. Junk #1 (selection bias): the treated group would have done differently anyway — healthier people take the gym membership. Junk #2 (heterogeneous-effect bias): the treatment helps the treated group by a different amount than it would help everyone else. A coin flip deciding who gets treated makes both junk terms average out to zero.


Randomization inference (RI). Fisher’s sharp null, \(H_0: \delta_i = 0\) for every \(i\), fills in every missing potential outcome (they equal the observed ones). Under it, you can recompute the test statistic for every possible assignment and get an exact \(p\)-value with no distributional assumptions and no appeal to large samples. It is the right tool for small experiments and a useful stress test for any design.






In plain English



Ask: “If the treatment did absolutely nothing to anyone, how often would a random reshuffle of who got treated produce a gap as big as the one I found?” You answer by actually doing the reshuffles — hundreds or thousands of them — and counting. If big gaps show up in 40% of reshuffles, your result is unremarkable; if they show up in 0.1%, it is not.

title: Session 5 · Regression discontinuity
text:
Key ideas
The design. Treatment \(D\) is a deterministic function of a running variable \(X\) relative to a cutoff \(c_0\): \(D = 1[X \geq c_0]\) (sharp regression discontinuity) or jumps in probability there (fuzzy). Units just above and just below the cutoff differ in treatment but, if nothing else jumps at \(c_0\), in nothing else.






In plain English



Some rule says: score 50 or above and you get the treatment, 49 and you don’t. A person at 49 and a person at 50 are practically identical — a little luck on the test is all that separates them — yet one got treated and one didn’t. Compare those two groups and you have something close to an experiment, at least near the line.


Identification by continuity. \(E[Y^0 \mid X]\) and \(E[Y^1 \mid X]\) must be continuous at \(c_0\). Then \[\delta_{SRD} = \lim_{x \downarrow c_0} E[Y \mid X = x] - \lim_{x \uparrow c_0} E[Y \mid X = x].\] No conditional-independence assumption, no need to observe confounders: everything that matters is a smooth function of \(X\) except the treatment.






In plain English



The only assumption is that nothing else changes abruptly at the cutoff. People’s background characteristics, motivation, whatever — all of it should drift smoothly across the line. If the outcome jumps at the line anyway, the treatment did it.


Estimation is a bias–variance problem. You need the two limits. Global polynomials use all the data but let far-away observations drive the fit at the cutoff (Gelman and Imbens’s warning against high-order polynomials). Local linear regression within a bandwidth \(h\) is the modern default, with rdrobust choosing \(h\) and correcting for bias. The honest report shows several.






In plain English



You want to know the height of the two curves exactly at the cutoff. Use lots of data far from the cutoff and you get a precise but possibly wrong answer, because far-away points bend the curve. Use only data close to the cutoff and you get the right shape but a noisier estimate. The bandwidth is that dial; show more than one setting.


Threats and checks. If units can precisely manipulate \(X\) (sorting just above a test-score cutoff), continuity fails. Check that the density of \(X\) is smooth at \(c_0\) (McCrary) and that pre-determined covariates do not jump there. Fuzzy RD is instrumental variables with the cutoff as instrument, which is next session’s topic.






In plain English



The design breaks if people can nudge themselves across the line — retaking a test until they pass, say. The tell-tale sign is a pile-up of observations just on the favorable side of the cutoff. Also check that things decided before treatment (age, prior income) don’t jump at the line; if they do, something other than the rule is going on.


The Lee–Moretti–Butler (LMB) question. Do close elections reveal whether politicians converge to the median voter (Downs) or diverge to their party’s preferences? In a 50–50 district the party that barely won is as-good-as random; if the winner’s voting score jumps at the 50% line, parties do not converge.

title: Session 7 · Panel data and the 2×2 difference-in-differences
text:
Key ideas
The fixed-effects (FE) model. \(Y_{it} = \delta D_{it} + \mathbf{X}_{it}\beta + u_i + \varepsilon_{it}\). The unit effect \(u_i\) can be correlated with \(D_{it}\) in any way; FE removes it by comparing each unit to itself across time. Three equivalent implementations: unit dummies, demeaning every variable within unit, or first-differencing (with two periods).






In plain English



If you watch the same people over time, you can ask “when this person’s treatment changed, did this person’s outcome change?” — and never compare one person to another at all. Everything that is permanently true about a person (their background, their baseline talent) cancels out, because it is the same in every period.


What FE needs. Strict exogeneity: \(E[\varepsilon_{it} \mid D_{i1}, \dots, D_{iT}, u_i] = 0\). Time-varying unobservables that move with \(D\) are still a problem. Reverse causality and feedback (today’s shock affects tomorrow’s treatment) violate it. FE also needs within variation; a regressor that never changes for a unit is absorbed.






In plain English



Fixed effects handle the things about a unit that never change. They do nothing about things that change over time alongside the treatment — a provider who raises prices and starts offering a riskier service in the same month because business got slow. And they can’t estimate the effect of anything that never varies for a given unit, because there is no “before and after” to compare.


The SASP question. Sex workers charge more for unprotected sex. Is that a compensating differential for risk, or do higher-priced providers simply differ in ways that also make them more likely to offer it? The Survey of Adult Service Providers (SASP) panel follows the same provider across clients, so provider-level unobservables drop out.
The 2×2 difference-in-differences (DiD). Two groups, two periods. \(\hat{\delta} = (\bar{Y}_{T,post} - \bar{Y}_{T,pre}) - (\bar{Y}_{C,post} - \bar{Y}_{C,pre})\). The identifying assumption is parallel trends: absent treatment, the treated group’s outcome would have moved by the same amount as the control group’s. It is a statement about a counterfactual and is untestable in the 2×2 case. As a regression: \(Y = \alpha + \beta\,\text{Treat} + \gamma\,\text{Post} + \delta\,(\text{Treat} \times \text{Post}) + e\).






In plain English



Before-and-after on its own is misleading, because things change over time for everyone. So take the treated group’s before-after change and subtract the control group’s before-after change; whatever is left over is the treatment. The hidden bet is that, without the treatment, both groups would have changed by the same amount — “parallel trends.”


John Snow. In 1854 London, the Lambeth water company had moved its intake upstream of the sewage; Southwark & Vauxhall had not. Cholera deaths fell in Lambeth-served households and rose elsewhere. It is the first DiD and still one of the cleanest.

title: Session 7 · Panel data and the 2×2 difference-in-differences
text:
Solutions






Solutions (click to expand)





1. With \(T = 2\), demeaning and differencing use the same single within-unit contrast, so the estimates coincide exactly (≈ −0.06 in this small subsample — note it has the opposite sign from the full-panel FE estimate, a reminder that 68 providers is not much data). Adding a constant to the FD regression is the same as adding a period fixed effect to the FE model. For \(T > 2\) FE uses all pairwise contrasts weighted by the within-unit variance, while FD uses only adjacent-period contrasts; they differ, and FD is more robust when \(\varepsilon_{it}\) is a random walk.
2. FE is biased because strict exogeneity fails: \(D_{it}\) depends on \(\varepsilon_{i,t-1}\), and demeaning puts every period’s \(\varepsilon\) into every period’s transformed error. The bias shrinks as \(T\) grows (it is of order \(1/T\)). First differencing also fails here, because \(\Delta D_{it}\) depends on \(\varepsilon_{i,t-1}\) which is in \(\Delta \varepsilon_{it}\).
rng = np.random.default_rng(0); N, T = 500, 5
e = rng.normal(size=(N, T)); D = np.zeros((N, T), int); D[:, 1:] = (e[:, :-1] > 0)
u = rng.normal(size=(N, 1)); Y = 1 * D + u + e
df = pd.DataFrame({"y": Y.ravel(), "d": D.ravel(), "i": np.repeat(np.arange(N), T), "t": np.tile(np.arange(T), N)})
dm = df.assign(y=df.y - df.groupby("i").y.transform("mean"), d=df.d - df.groupby("i").d.transform("mean"))
print(smf.ols("y ~ d", dm).fit().params["d"])    # noticeably below 1
3. Chelsea vs S&V: \((125 - 110) - (147 - 135) = 3\): two untreated companies moved in parallel. That is evidence consistent with parallel trends for the untreated, which makes the assumption more plausible for Lambeth. It does not test Lambeth’s own counterfactual trend, which is unobservable by construction.

title: Session 9 · Synthetic control, and which design when
text:
Key ideas
The comparative case study. One treated aggregate unit (a state, a country), a handful of candidate controls, and a long pre-period. Difference-in-differences (DiD) with one treated unit has no credible standard error and picks the control arbitrarily. Synthetic control replaces the choice with an algorithm: find weights \(w_j \geq 0\), \(\sum w_j = 1\), over donor units \(j\) that make the weighted average of donors match the treated unit’s pre-treatment outcomes and predictors as closely as possible. The post-period gap between the treated unit and its synthetic version is the estimated effect.






In plain English



Texas did something; no other single state is a fair comparison. So build a “fake Texas” by blending other states — 56% Florida, 27% New York, 17% Illinois — with the blend chosen so that fake Texas tracked real Texas closely for the nine years before the policy. If the two then split apart after the policy, the gap is your estimate.


Why the constraints matter. Non-negativity and summing to one keep the synthetic unit inside the convex hull of the donors: no extrapolation, and the weights are interpretable (“Texas is 56% Florida, 27% New York…”). A poor pre-period fit means the method has nothing to say; report the pre-period root mean squared prediction error (RMSPE).






In plain English



The weights have to be positive and add up to 100%, which means fake Texas is a genuine blend — not “three Californias minus two Floridas,” which would be numerically fine and meaningless. And if the blend never tracked real Texas well before the policy, the comparison afterwards is worthless; the pre-period fit number is the first thing to report.


Inference by placebo. Reassign treatment to each donor in turn, fit its synthetic control, and compute its post/pre RMSPE ratio. If the treated unit’s ratio is extreme relative to the placebo distribution, the effect is unlikely to be luck. The “p-value” is the treated unit’s rank divided by the number of units.






In plain English



Pretend Florida was the treated state and build a fake Florida; see how big a post-period gap you get by chance. Do that for all fifty states. If real Texas’s gap (relative to how well its fake tracked it beforehand) is the biggest of the fifty-one, the odds of that happening by luck are about one in fifty-one.


The Texas question. Texas massively expanded prison capacity in 1993–1994. Black male incarceration roughly doubled over the following years. Did the building cause the filling, relative to a synthetic Texas built from other states?
What the book wants you to leave with. Every chapter answered the same question: where does the exogenous variation come from? Randomization (Ch. 4), observable selection you can model (Ch. 5), a threshold (Ch. 6), an instrument (Ch. 7), within-unit change (Ch. 8), a policy difference across groups and time (Ch. 9), a weighted comparison unit (Ch. 10). The method follows the source of variation, never the reverse.






In plain English



Every design in this book is an answer to one question: what decided who got the treatment, and was it anything like a coin flip? An actual coin flip, a cutoff rule, a quirk of geography, a change over time, a policy that hit some places and not others. Find that first; the method follows from it. If you can’t find it, no method will manufacture it.

Step 3 — Placebo-in-space inference

PythonR



def fit_state(st):
    d = Dataprep(foo=tx, dependent="bmprison", unit_variable="statefip", time_variable="year",
                 treatment_identifier=st, controls_identifier=[s for s in tx.statefip.unique() if s != st],
                 predictors=["poverty", "income"], predictors_op="mean", time_predictors_prior=range(1985, 1994),
                 special_predictors=dp.special_predictors, time_optimize_ssr=range(1985, 1994))
    s = Synth(); s.fit(dataprep=d, optim_method="BFGS", optim_initial="ols")
    Z0, Z1 = d.make_outcome_mats(time_period=range(1985, 2001)); g = Z1 - Z0 @ s.W
    pre  = np.sqrt((g.loc[1985:1993] ** 2).mean())
    post = np.sqrt((g.loc[1994:2000] ** 2).mean())
    return pd.Series({"pre_rmspe": pre, "post_rmspe": post, "ratio": post / pre})

Step 4 — Wrap-up: which design, when
Put three fresh questions to the room and make the group pick a design and name its key assumption and its first diagnostic. Suggested questions:

Did a city’s new minimum-wage ordinance reduce restaurant employment? — difference-in-differences or synthetic control against comparable cities; parallel trends / pre-period fit; event-study leads or placebo-in-space.
Does an extra year of schooling raise earnings for students who barely pass a school-entry test? — regression discontinuity (RDD) on the test score; continuity at the cutoff; density test and covariate smoothness.
Do defendants assigned public defenders get longer sentences than those with private counsel? — Selection on unobservables is severe; an instrumental variable (IV) such as random assignment of public-defender availability (judge-leniency style); relevance and exclusion; first-stage F and a complier description.

Then the decision tree, in words. If treatment was randomized, compare means and use randomization inference. If selection is on observables you can defend with a DAG, match or weight, and check overlap. If treatment switches at a threshold, RD. If something exogenous shifts treatment but not the outcome, IV, and say whose effect you are estimating. If you observe units before and after a change, fixed effects or DiD, with an event study to show the pre-period. If you have one treated aggregate and a long pre-period, synthetic control with placebo inference. If none of those apply, the honest answer is that the data cannot answer the causal question, and that is a finding.

Exercises

Leave-one-out. Drop Florida (the largest-weight donor) from the donor pool and refit the synthetic Texas. How much do the weights and the post-period gap change? Then also drop the state with the next-largest weight. What does sensitivity to a single donor tell you?
Placebo-in-time. Pretend treatment happened in 1989 and fit the synthetic control using only 1985–1988 to choose weights. Is there a spurious “effect” after 1989? Why is this a useful check in addition to placebo-in-space?
Design memo. Pick a causal question from your own work. In one page: state the estimand (average effect for everyone, for the treated, for compliers, or local to a cutoff — ATE, ATT, LATE, or RD…), the design you would use, its identifying assumption written as a counterfactual statement, two diagnostics you would show, and the one thing that would make you abandon the design.

Solutions






Solutions (click to expand)





1. Without Florida the weight shifts to Illinois (0.44), New York (0.35) and California (0.21); the post-period gap is ≈ 23,600 and the pre-RMSPE rises only slightly (≈ 1,050). Dropping New York as well leaves Illinois 0.56 / California 0.44, a gap of ≈ 23,000 and pre-RMSPE ≈ 1,250. The result is not an artifact of any one donor. Large sensitivity to one donor would mean the synthetic unit was really a single comparison state, and you would be back to a one-control DiD.
2. With a 1989 pseudo-treatment, the synthetic and actual series continue to track through 1993, with no gap that resembles the post-1993 one. Placebo-in-time guards against the pre-period fit being achieved by overfitting a short window; placebo-in-space guards against the post-period gap being within the range of ordinary noise.
3. Discussed in the meeting. A good memo names the counterfactual explicitly (“absent the ordinance, employment in city A would have followed the trend in cities B–D”).

Facilitator notes






Facilitator notes (click to expand)





Run Step 3 before the meeting. The 51-fit placebo loop takes several minutes in Python; have the results table ready and only re-run the Texas fit live. tidysynth with generate_placebos = TRUE does the loop inside generate_weights().
Misconception: the weights are “the” comparison states. They are the solution to an optimization with the predictors you chose. Change the predictors and the weights move (Step 1’s expect box shows this between implementations). What should not move much is the post-period gap.
Misconception: a pre-period fit that looks good is good enough. Insist on the pre-RMSPE number and the placebo-in-time check. Synthetic control with a short or badly fitted pre-period is a very elaborate way of picking a control state by hand.

Regression anatomy: “controlling for” is mechanical
The open question: which variables should you control for?

Nodes are variables; \(A \to B\) means \(A\) causes \(B\)

title: Matching and subclassification
text:
Last time

SDO = ATE + selection bias + HTE bias
Randomization kills both. Without it?
Today’s bet: we can see everything that drives selection

title: Matching and subclassification
text:
Conditional independence
\[(Y^0, Y^1) \perp D \mid X\]

Within strata of \(X\), treatment is as good as random
The backdoor criterion, in potential-outcomes clothing
Untestable: it is a claim about unobservables

title: Matching and subclassification
text:
Common support
\[0 < P(D = 1 \mid X) < 1\]

Every covariate profile needs both treated and untreated units
Without it you are extrapolating, not matching
The one assumption you can check — so check it

title: Matching and subclassification
text:
Subclassification

Stratify on \(X\); difference in means within each stratum
Average with the treated group’s stratum shares → ATT
Works with 2–3 discrete covariates
Dies of the curse of dimensionality immediately after

title: Matching and subclassification

title: Matching and subclassification

The propensity score

\(p(X) = P(D = 1 \mid X)\)
Rosenbaum & Rubin: if CIA holds given \(X\), it holds given \(p(X)\)
One number replaces the whole vector
Estimate with a logit; then stratify, weight (IPW), or match on it

title: Matching and subclassification

Not a prediction problem

You are not trying to predict treatment well
A score with perfect separation means no overlap
The goal is covariate balance, and the diagnostic is the balance table

title: Instrumental variables
text:
LATE

With heterogeneous effects, IV identifies the effect for compliers: units whose \(D\) is moved by \(Z\)
Different instruments → different compliers → different LATEs
Card’s compliers: people for whom college distance was binding
Stevenson’s compliers: defendants detained by a strict judge, released by a lenient one

IV is reduced form over first stage. Relevance you can test; exclusion you must argue; and the answer is a LATE for whoever the instrument moves.

title: Difference-in-differences, deep dive
text:
Last time

The 2×2: no standard errors, no test of parallel trends
Today: many periods, many groups — and a new problem

title: Difference-in-differences, deep dive
text:
Event studies


One coefficient per year relative to 1985. Flat before 1986 (nothing was happening yet); a parabola during the years the treated cohorts were 15–19; back to zero after.

title: Difference-in-differences, deep dive
text:
Placebos and triple differences

If theory says the effect exists only for a group / cohort / window, estimate it where it should not and demand zero
DDD: subtract the placebo group’s DD from the treated group’s DD
Absorbs group-specific shocks a plain DD would call “treatment”

title: Difference-in-differences, deep dive
text:
Abortion legalization (Cunningham & Cornwell 2013)

Five states repealed bans in 1970; Roe in 1973
Treated cohorts: born 1971–73 in repeal states
Prediction: lower gonorrhea among 15–19 year olds in 1986–92, tracing a parabola as the cohort ages through the bracket
Placebo: 25–29 year olds

title: Difference-in-differences, deep dive
text:
Staggered adoption


TWFE: \(Y_{it} = \alpha_i + \lambda_t + \delta D_{it} + e_{it}\)
Goodman-Bacon: \(\hat{\delta}\) is a weighted average of every 2×2 among these groups — including late-treated vs already-treated

title: Difference-in-differences, deep dive
text:
What the decomposition shows


Here the forbidden comparisons carry 2% of the weight, so TWFE is safe. With no never-treated states, that share can dominate.

title: Difference-in-differences, deep dive
text:
Modern estimators

Callaway–Sant’Anna: ATT for each cohort × period, using only never- or not-yet-treated controls; aggregate with chosen weights
Sun–Abraham: the same idea inside an interaction-weighted event-study regression
Both need a clean control group; neither is magic

title: Difference-in-differences, deep dive
text:
Castle doctrine (Cheng & Hoekstra 2013)

“Stand your ground” laws, 2005–2010, 21 states
TWFE: log homicide up ≈ 8%
29 never-treated states → the decomposition puts 90% of weight on clean comparisons

title: Difference-in-differences, deep dive
text:
Takeaway

The event-study plot is the deliverable. TWFE is a weighted average with weights you did not choose; decompose it, and if the forbidden comparisons carry weight, use an estimator that refuses to make them.
